name: Maasai
subtitle: Maasai: who the sources name, where they live, and what the old labels got wrong.

keyPoints.text: About 1,189,522 people (2019): Kenya only: people counted as Maasai by ethnic community in the 2019 Kenya Population and Housing Census, as reported by the press from KNBS results (KNBS table itself not read).
Kenya's census counted 154,906 Maasai in 1969 (1.43% of the population) and 1,189,522 in 2019 (about 2.5%), roughly seven-fold.
Glottolog lists Maasai as a language of Kenya and Tanzania, classified within Eastern Nilotic (Nuclear Maa) and not endangered.

parts.text: Glottolog lists Maasai as a language of Kenya and Tanzania, classified within Eastern Nilotic (Nuclear Maa) and not endangered.
A Mara study (2012) says leasing land to tourism investors through conservancies can keep rangeland areas together, but subdivision of Kenya's rangelands has tended to benefit elites.
The Southern Reserve created after 1904 lay on the border with German East Africa (now Tanzania).

items.text: Maasai elders signed the 1904 agreement with the British, which was pledged to last 'so long as the Maasai as a race shall exist'; several sections were moved into Laikipia and a Southern Reserve.

Maasai plaintiffs challenged the agreements in court; the High Court dismissed the case in May 1913 and the appeal failed in December 1913, the judges treating the agreements as treaties (Acts of State).

Amnesty International says Maasai were moved from Serengeti National Park to Loliondo in 1959 and were later repeatedly evicted. (Paraphrase from a reading of the page; exact wording not captured, verify before use.)

Nine UN experts said a plan to turn 1,500 of 4,000 sq km of Loliondo village land into a game reserve could displace up to 70,000 Maasai, and that about 80,000 more faced eviction from the Ngorongoro Conservation Area; they cited reports of live ammunition and tear gas on 10 June.

Amnesty International reported that 27 Maasai were charged over a police officer's killing and 132 arrested for alleged illegal presence; all were later discharged for lack of evidence (Amnesty's account).
Human Rights Watch reported that Tanzania aims to relocate over 82,000 people from Ngorongoro to Msomera, about 600 km away; the government says the scheme complies with national rights laws.
